text: Paper overview: Field, Goldsmith & Habing (1969) → Chapter 02 / FGH & GHF 1969 / Model ingredients From historical rates to the two-phase curve. Field’s stability theory tells us when perturbations grow. The next question is what determines the equilibrium state of the gas. Here we begin with the historical heating expressions and metal cooling coefficients behind the 1969 two-phase model. Scope: validated model ingredients. These new diagnostic plots evaluate published formulas; they are not reproductions of Figures 1 and 2 in the FGH Letter. A new cold-to-warm equilibrium prototype now shows the S-shaped pressure curves. A 96-point original-figure comparison and stopping note now document the residual mismatch; further historical coefficient recovery is deferred; the earlier reduced cold branch is retained for comparison. The cold and warm branches now connect. The new coupled calculation includes superthermal electrons, secondary hydrogen ionization, and thermal hydrogen excitation and ionization. It produces temperature, pressure, and electron-density curves for normal abundances and the two FGH depletion cases. Explore the two-phase equilibrium prototype → Its 48 numerical checks test the equations as implemented. Remaining atomic-data and recombination conventions are explicit; numerical agreement is not yet historical validation. Two papers, one model The Letter and its detailed companion. Field, Goldsmith & Habing (FGH), ApJ 155, L149–L154, presents the equilibrium temperature, pressure, and electron-density curves. Goldsmith, Habing & Field (GHF), ApJ 158, 173–184, explicitly calls that Letter “Paper I” and describes the heating, cooling, and ionization calculation in more detail. The companion paper supplies the equations and Table 1 used below. Keeping the two sources distinct matters: some printed depletion parameters differ between them. How much ionization energy becomes heat? Derived diagnostics from GHF (1969), equations (25)–(26), printed p. 181. Both curves depend on x = ne/n(H I). Their denominators differ: energy per primary liberated electron is not the same quantity as the fraction of total ionization-plus-excitation losses. SVGPNGHeating data / CSV Q(x) = (1 + 130x)/(1 + 57x) eh = 9Q eV · f = 0.13Q The electron fraction changes how energetic electrons share their energy with the gas. Equation (26) gives approximately 9, 13, and 20 eV at x = 10⁻⁴, 10⁻², and 1. The printed fit slightly exceeds 20 eV near x = 1; the code preserves the historical rounded expression. Equation (23) separately gives Γion/(ζntarget) = 1.4 × 10⁻¹¹Q erg. Here ntarget = n(H I) + n(He I) + n(He II) is the density of primary-ionization targets in equation (20), distinct from the H+He nuclei density n0, and ζ is the cosmic-ray ionization rate. Direct electron heating is another term, Γel = 4.6 × 10⁻¹⁰neζ erg cm⁻³ s⁻¹. It is not added to the plotted energy without specifying the particle populations. Rounded coefficients in the paper are retained independently: the 0.13 in equation (25) is not forced to equal 1.4/11 from the prefactors of equations (23)–(24). The historical metal cooling coefficients. GHF (1969), Table 1, printed p. 179, and equation (16), p. 178. The chosen temperature range evaluates the formulas; it does not independently establish their accuracy over that entire range. Coefficients below 10⁻²⁹ are clipped in the display, while the CSV preserves log₁₀ values. SVGPNGCooling data / CSVTranscribed coefficients / JSON rk(T) = RTmexp(−T*/T) Λ2 = Σknk(nerek + nHrHk) These r values have units of erg cm³ s⁻¹: they are energy-loss coefficients, rather than bare excitation probabilities. The relative total cooling contributions require target populations, collider densities, and elemental abundances. A large coefficient alone does not identify the dominant coolant. Five electron fits and six H-atom fits are transcribed from the table. Missing entries remain unavailable. In particular, a blank for a collider is not treated as a measured zero. An input discrepancy to resolve Keep the printed depletion cases separate. The FGH Figure 1 caption gives Fe depletion factors 4 and 10 for cases a and b. The detailed GHF paper, section IV on p. 180, lists remaining Fe fractions 0.3 and 0.01, corresponding to depletion factors approximately 3.33 and 100. Both statements are recorded in the source audit, along with the other elements. The original equilibrium curves will require a deliberate choice and justification; the ingredient plots do not use either depletion case. An equilibrium experiment Take the ingredients into a coupled cold-gas solution. Our next exhibit solves charge neutrality and thermal balance in a restricted 10–2,000 K window. It compares three abundance cases and two electron-donor prescriptions, with downloadable populations and heating/cooling budgets.
